USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Enter the Beijing talks (beginning this very weekend, May 3-4) with a clear objective of brokering a short-term truce — an agreement to keep the proposed Section 301 tariffs on hold while China commits to concrete near-term measures (increased purchases of US agricultural and energy goods, phased opening of autos/financial sectors) — while preserving the credibility of the tariff threat as leverage. Do not escalate or impose the $50B list during the negotiating window, and do not reach for a maximal structural settlement that Beijing has already ruled out. This protects our export and farm-belt economy while keeping pressure on China's core trade practices.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat is real but bounded, so I rate it +0.4 rather than existential. The US has initiated this confrontation, and it now carries direct, material two-way exposure: China has targeted our retaliation-sensitive exports — soybeans (the #2 US export to China and China is our #1 agricultural market), pork, autos, aircraft — precisely at Trump's political base, with farm-belt alarm already threatening GOP losses in competitive 2018 midterm Senate/House races. The ZTE denial order (Apr 16) and the proposed ~$50B ICT/aerospace/robotics tariff list (Apr 3) add supply-chain and tech-leadership risk. Offsetting this, the US domestic economy at the decision date is strong — industrial production rising (103.3 Apr), consumer sentiment ~98, 10Y at 2.97%, fed funds 1.70% — and neither side's tariffs are yet in force (US comment period runs to May 22), so the situation is not yet an existential or material-GDP-drag outcome. The action stance (0.0, negotiate) follows from the risk calculus: escalating now would hand Beijing the farm-belt weapon and roil markets, while conceding structural points Beijing refuses (Made in China 2025) is a non-starter; the sensible path is to use the standing tariff threat as a bargaining chip to extract short-term Chinese purchases and opening commitments that defuse the immediate conflict ahead of midterms, and keep talking.
key_factors: US proposed ~$50B Section 301 tariff list (Apr 3) + ZTE ban (Apr 16) = active US escalation, but tariffs not yet in force (comment period to May 22)
China retaliation targeted US farm belt: $3B pork/fruit (Apr 2) and ~$50B incl. soybeans, autos, aircraft (Apr 4) — soybeans are #2 US export to China
Farm-belt political risk: GOP-held competitive 2018 midterm seats in soybean states threatened by trade war — domestic pressure to de-escalate
US economy strong at decision date: IP 103.3, sentiment ~98, 10Y 2.97%, fed funds 1.70% — no recession signal, US holds leverage
High-level US delegation (Mnuchin/Lighthizer/Kudlow/Navarro) entering Beijing talks May 3-4; expectations slim, delegation internally split
China refuses structural concessions on core interests/Made in China 2025; offers only short-term purchase and opening measures

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR publishes proposed Section 301 tariff list: ~1,300 Chinese product lines (~$50B), targeting aerospace, ICT, robotics, machinery.
China announces proposed retaliatory tariffs on ~$50B of US goods (soybeans, automobiles, aircraft).
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). Major non-tariff escalation.
China's proposed tariffs on soybeans would hit hardest in Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Indiana, Missouri, North Dakota — competitive 2018 races; farm belt could cost Republicans midterms.
Most likely outcome for US-China talks launching Thursday is agreement to keep talking, Trump maintaining threat of punitive tariffs.
US has threatened tariffs on more than $150B of Chinese imports; China threatened tariffs on more than $50B of US imports, ~39% of US goods sent to China.
US industrial production 103.3 in April 2018, rising; economy strong, no recession signal.
